Reading and adapting patterns

Before you make anything big, you must be able to read a pattern from any country, check your gauge, and change the size to fit a real body. This module turns pattern reading into a calm, step-by-step routine with simple arithmetic you can do on a phone calculator.

Sizes in brackets work like a code. If a pattern says *Cast on 88 (96, 104, 112) sts* and you are making the third size, you cast on 104. A quick trick: before you start, take a pencil (or a screenshot and the markup tool on your phone) and circle every number for your size through the whole pattern. You will never read the wrong number in the middle of a row.
Repeats: asterisks and brackets
**Asterisk repeat:** *k2, p2; rep from * to end* means work k2, p2 again and again until no stitches are left.
**To last stitches:** *rep from * to last 2 sts, k2* means stop repeating when only 2 stitches remain, then work those 2 as told.
**Brackets or parentheses:** (yo, k2tog) 5 times means work that group exactly 5 times.
**Stitch count:** a number at the end of a row, like (48 sts), is your checkpoint. Count after every shaping row.

The same name means different stitches. A US single crochet is a UK double crochet. If you follow a US pattern with UK stitches, every stitch is one step too tall and the piece grows longer and wider than planned. Look for clues: US patterns use sc and hdc; UK patterns use htr and say tension and miss instead of gauge and skip.

Knitting terms are nearly the same in both countries. The main differences are words: *cast off* (UK) and *bind off* (US), *tension* and *gauge*, and *stocking stitch* and *stockinette*. Knitting needle sizes are given in millimetres in most modern patterns; older US patterns may use US numbers, so always check the millimetre size.
Worked example: converting and checking two pattern lines
For example, Amaka in Owerri has a free American crochet pattern for a table mat and a British knitting pattern for a cushion. She checks both before buying yarn.
Crochet line (US): Row 1: sc in 2nd ch from hook and in each ch across (20 sc). Row 2: ch 2, hdc in each st across.
She rewrites it in UK terms on a card: Row 1: dc in 2nd ch from hook and each ch across (20 dc). Row 2: ch 2, htr in each st across.
Knitting line (UK): cast on 22 sts. Row 1: *k2, p2; rep from * to last 2 sts, k2.
She checks the arithmetic: 22 minus the last 2 leaves 20 stitches for the repeat. 20 divided by 4 (k2, p2 is 4 stitches) is exactly 5 repeats, then k2. The numbers fit.
She notes the row ends with k2, so the next row will begin with the stitches matching k2 on the other side, which makes a neat 2 by 2 rib.
Amaka works the mat with the correct short stitches, and she knows her rib repeat fits before she starts. If 20 had not divided by 4, she would have known the cast-on number was wrong for her size.
Reading a chart

A chart is a grid where **each square is one stitch** and each row of squares is one row of knitting or crochet. The key beside it explains each symbol. The Craft Yarn Council publishes standard symbols, but designers sometimes use their own, so always read the key.
Find row 1. It is at the **bottom** of the chart, because fabric grows upward.

For flat knitting, read right-side rows from **right to left**, and wrong-side rows from **left to right**. The row numbers on the edge usually show this: odd numbers on the right, even numbers on the left.
For knitting in the round, read **every** row from right to left, because you always face the right side.
A red or bold box marks the pattern repeat. Work the stitches inside the box as many times as the row needs.
Use a ruler, a strip of paper or a sticky note **above** the row you are working, so you can see the rows already done below it.

Gauge swatches: making, blocking, measuring and fixing your tension
Make a gauge swatch in the correct stitch, needle or hook and yarn
Block and measure the swatch accurately across a wide span
Calculate how far off your finished piece will be if gauge does not match
Decide whether to change needle or hook size and by how much

**Gauge** (called **tension** in UK patterns) is how many stitches and rows fit into 10 cm of your fabric. It is the link between the pattern's numbers and real centimetres. Two women can use the same yarn and the same 4 mm needles and get different gauge, because everyone holds yarn a little differently. That is why a careful designer gives a gauge, and why a careful maker checks it.
A straight ruler
A rigid ruler, not a soft tape, gives the most reliable gauge reading.
How to make a swatch you can trust
Use the **same yarn** you will use for the project, and the needle or hook size the pattern suggests.
Make the swatch **bigger than 10 cm**: about 15 cm square. Edges are always uneven, so you measure only the middle.
Work in the **stitch named in the gauge line**. If the gauge says 'in stocking stitch', a garter stitch swatch tells you nothing.
If the project is knitted in the round, swatch in the round or use a quick 'speed swatch' method, because many people knit and purl at different tensions.
**Block it the way you will wash the finished item**: soak in cool water, press out water in a towel, lay flat and let it dry completely. Cotton and many plant fibres can change after washing.
Measuring: go wide, then divide

Lay the dry swatch flat on a table without stretching it. Put the ruler across the middle and count stitches between two pins placed some distance apart. Counting over 15 cm and dividing is more accurate than counting over 10 cm, because a half stitch matters. In knitting, each V is one stitch. In crochet, count the tops of the stitches, and count rows by the height of each row of posts.
Worked example: what a 2-stitch difference does to a jumper
For example, Funke in Ibadan is making a cotton jumper. The pattern gauge is 22 stitches and 30 rows to 10 cm in stocking stitch on 4 mm needles. The front is 110 stitches wide.
She knits a 30-stitch swatch on 4 mm needles, washes it and dries it flat.
She places pins 15 cm apart and counts 30 stitches. 30 divided by 15 is 2.0 stitches per cm, which is 20 stitches per 10 cm.
Pattern width of the front: 110 stitches divided by 2.2 stitches per cm = 50 cm.
Her width with her gauge: 110 divided by 2.0 = 55 cm.
Front and back together will be 10 cm larger around her body than the pattern says.
She changes to 3.5 mm needles, knits a new swatch and counts 33 stitches in 15 cm. 33 divided by 15 is 2.2 stitches per cm: exactly 22 per 10 cm.
By spending one evening on two swatches, Funke avoids a jumper that would have been 10 cm too big around. She now knits the pattern exactly as written on 3.5 mm needles.

Stitch gauge usually matters more than row gauge, because most patterns tell you to work 'until piece measures 30 cm', so you control length with a tape measure. Row gauge matters a lot in top-down yokes, sleeve shaping and colourwork charts, where the pattern counts rows to make shapes.
Yarn weight standards help you guess

The Craft Yarn Council's Standard Yarn Weight System numbers yarns from 0 (lace) to 7 (jumbo). For example, a medium (4) worsted or aran-type yarn is usually knitted at roughly 16 to 20 stitches per 10 cm, and a light (3) DK yarn at roughly 21 to 24. These ranges are a starting guide; your swatch is the final word.

Keep your swatches. Pin a small paper tag to each one with the yarn name, needle or hook size, stitches and rows per 10 cm, and the date. After a few months you will have a personal library that shows how you knit or crochet with the yarns sold in your local market. That library saves money, because you will often know the right needle before you even start.
Gauge can change mid-project

Tension often loosens when you relax or tightens when you are tired or worried. Measure your work again after the first 10 cm of a large piece. If it has drifted, change needle size now, not at the end.
Swatch in the right stitch and yarn, about 15 cm square, and wash it before measuring.
Count across a wide span and divide; half a stitch per centimetre changes the size a lot.
Width = stitches divided by your stitches per cm: use this to predict the real size.
Too many stitches: go up a needle or hook size. Too few: go down.

Resizing a pattern with gauge arithmetic and stitch repeats
Calculate a new stitch count from a target measurement and your gauge
Adjust the count so it fits the stitch pattern repeat

Sometimes the pattern's sizes do not match the body you are making for. The bust may fit but the hips are tight, or the size range stops below the size you need. You do not have to give up on the pattern. Knitting and crochet are made of countable units, so you can resize with three simple formulas and some careful checking.
A person working through calculations on a board
Resizing is careful arithmetic: target centimetres, gauge, then the stitch repeat.
The three formulas
**Stitches = target width in cm x stitches per cm.** Stitches per cm is your gauge divided by 10.
**Rows = target length in cm x rows per cm.**
**Yarn needed rises roughly in proportion to the stitches.** If you make a piece 20% wider, plan for about 20% more yarn for that piece.

Always start from the **finished measurement you want**, not the body measurement. A cardigan for a person with a 102 cm bust might need a finished bust of 110 cm so that it sits comfortably. The difference is called **ease**, and you will study it in detail in Module 4. For now, look at the pattern's schematic (the small drawing with measurements) to see how much ease the designer planned, and keep a similar amount.
Fitting the stitch repeat

Most stitch patterns are written as *a multiple of X plus Y*. For example, a cable rib might need a multiple of 6 stitches plus 2. That means the stitch count, minus 2, must divide exactly by 6. If your calculated number does not fit, move to the nearest number that does, and check what width that gives. Never just add one or two stitches to the middle of a repeat, or the pattern will look broken.
Worked example: resizing a cardigan back

For example, Grace in Jos wants to make a cabled cardigan. The largest size has a back of 46 cm (92 stitches at 20 stitches per 10 cm). The person she is making for needs a finished bust of about 112 cm, so the back should be about 56 cm. The cable rib is a multiple of 6 plus 2. Her gauge matches the pattern.
Stitches per cm: 20 divided by 10 = 2.
Target back stitches: 56 cm x 2 = 112 stitches.
Check the repeat: 112 minus 2 = 110. 110 divided by 6 = 18.33, so 112 does not fit.
Nearest numbers that fit: 18 repeats x 6 + 2 = 110 stitches, or 19 x 6 + 2 = 116 stitches.
Widths: 110 divided by 2 = 55 cm; 116 divided by 2 = 58 cm. She chooses 110 stitches, giving a finished bust of 110 cm, which still allows about 8 cm of ease over a 102 cm bust.
Length: she wants the body 5 cm longer. Row gauge is 28 rows per 10 cm, so 5 x 2.8 = 14 extra rows, added in the plain section before the armholes, not in the shaping.
Yarn: 110 divided by 92 = about 1.2, so roughly 20% more. The pattern asks for 8 balls, and 8 x 1.2 = 9.6. With the extra length she buys 11 balls from the same dye lot.
Grace casts on 110 stitches for the back, adds 14 rows before the armhole, and has enough yarn from one dye lot. The cable pattern stays complete across the whole back.

When you make the body wider, the shoulders and neck may also get wider unless you add the extra stitches into the armhole shaping. Draw a small schematic with your new numbers before you start, and check that the shoulders on front and back are still the same width.

In crochet the same formulas work, but crochet stitches are bigger, so each stitch you add or remove changes the width more. A double crochet in US terms might be about 0.5 to 0.7 cm wide in a medium yarn, so rounding by one repeat of 4 stitches could change a piece by over 2 cm. Recheck the width every time you round.

A **cable** is made by knitting a few stitches out of order. You slip some stitches onto a short spare needle called a **cable needle**, knit the next stitches, then knit the ones you set aside. The stitches cross over each other and form a rope. Repeat the crossing every few rows and the rope grows up the fabric. Cables look difficult, but each crossing is only four small moves.

A simple memory aid: **front goes left, back goes right**. If you always cross the same way, the rope twists in one direction like a spiral. If you put a C6B cable on the left of a panel and a C6F cable on the right, the two ropes mirror each other, which looks balanced on the front of a jumper or bag.

Worked example: a mirrored cable swatch
For example, Halima in Kaduna wants to test a cable panel for cushion covers she will sell. She uses a smooth, light-coloured medium yarn because cables show best in plain, pale yarn.
She plans the panel: p3, k6, p2, k6, p3. Total stitches: 3 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 3 = 20.
She adds 3 seed stitch stitches each side as a border, so she casts on 20 + 6 = 26 stitches.
Seed stitch on 3 stitches is k1, p1, k1 on every row, because each stitch is knitted where it shows a purl bump and purled where it shows a smooth knit V.
On wrong-side rows she knits the purl panel stitches and purls the k6 stitches, so the cables stay smooth.
Every 8th row she crosses: C6B on the first rope and C6F on the second, so they mirror.
After 4 crossings (32 rows) she lays the swatch flat and measures it.

Her 26-stitch swatch measures narrower than a plain stocking stitch swatch with the same number of stitches. She notes this because a cable cushion needs more stitches than a plain one of the same width.
Cables pull in

Crossed stitches overlap, so cabled fabric is narrower than stocking stitch with the same stitch count. Designers often increase a few stitches after the ribbing, before the cables start. Always swatch the cable pattern itself, not plain stocking stitch, when your project is mostly cables.
Reading a cable chart

On a cable chart, each plain square is one stitch: an empty square usually means knit on the right side, and a dot means purl on the right side. A cable crossing is shown as a long symbol stretching across 4 or 6 squares, with slanting lines that show which way the rope leans. The key will say which symbol is a front cross and which is a back cross. Count the rows between two crossing symbols: that number is your crossing interval.

Seed stitch: texture without a cable needle

**Seed stitch** (called moss stitch in UK patterns) alternates knit and purl, and moves by one stitch every row so bumps sit over flat stitches. On an odd number of stitches, every row is simply *k1, p1* ending k1. It lies flat, does not curl, and looks the same on both sides, which makes it a good border for cabled pieces and dishcloths.
Fixing a wrong crossing

If you find a cable crossed the wrong way a few rows down, you do not always have to undo every row. Experienced knitters drop just the cable stitches down to the wrong row, recross them, and work them back up with a crochet hook. Practise this on a swatch first, with a lifeline thread through a row below the mistake.

Worked example: planning a striped scarf and its yarn

For example, Kemi in Lagos is making a striped scarf in three colours for a school's old-girls' reunion. She wants it about 160 cm long. Her row gauge is 30 rows per 10 cm. A plain scarf in this yarn would use about 300 g.
Rows for 160 cm: 160 x 3 rows per cm = 480 rows.
Stripe sequence: 6 rows of colour A, 6 of B, 6 of C = 18 rows per repeat.
Repeats: 480 divided by 18 = 26.7. She rounds up to 27 repeats = 486 rows, about 162 cm, and ends on a full stripe.
Each colour is one third of the rows, so each uses about 300 g divided by 3 = 100 g.
Yarn is sold in 50 g balls, so she buys 2 balls of each colour, plus 1 extra ball of colour A for fringe and to be safe.
Kemi knows her stripe count and buys 7 balls instead of guessing. Every scarf she makes for the group will match because the sequence is written down.
Intarsia: one bobbin per block

In intarsia, count how many separate areas of colour cross each row. A block letter H in the centre of a cushion front crosses five areas on some rows: background, left leg, background, right leg, background. That means five bobbins, not two balls. Stranded knitting and float length

In stranded knitting, you knit with one colour and carry the other loosely behind. The carried strand is called a **float**. If floats are too tight, the fabric puckers and loses its stretch; if they are too long, fingers and rings catch on them. A widely used guide is not to leave a float longer than about 5 stitches (roughly 2.5 cm in medium yarn) without catching it by twisting it once with the working yarn. Before each colour change, spread the stitches on your right needle to their natural width so the float is long enough.
Hold one colour in each hand

Many stranded knitters hold the background colour in one hand and the pattern colour in the other. This keeps the colours from tangling and keeps one colour always on top, which gives a smoother result.

For hot climates, stranded fabric is thick because it is effectively two layers of yarn. It suits bags, cushion covers, hats for cool harmattan mornings and decorative bands rather than everyday tops. Intarsia keeps a single layer, so it works on lighter pieces.

Lace is fabric with holes placed on purpose. Each hole is made by a **yarn over**, which also adds a stitch. To keep the piece the same width, every yarn over is paired with a **decrease** that removes a stitch. Where you put the holes and which way the decreases lean create leaves, waves and diamonds. Light lace scarves and shawls in cotton or bamboo-type yarns suit warm weather and sell well as gifts.
A ball of yarn

For example, Ruth in Abuja wants to make cotton lace scarves for a bridal party. She writes her own simple pattern. Right-side rows: k2, *yo, ssk, k1, k2tog, yo, k1; rep from * to last 3 sts, k3. Wrong-side rows: k2, purl to last 2 sts, k2.
She counts one repeat: yo (+1), ssk (minus 1), k1 (0), k2tog (minus 1), yo (+1), k1 (0). Net change is 0, and the repeat is 6 stitches.
Edges: 2 stitches before the repeats and 3 after, so the cast-on is 6 x repeats + 5.
She wants about 7 repeats: 6 x 7 + 5 = 47 stitches.
Her swatch gauge after blocking is 20 stitches per 10 cm, so 47 stitches gives about 23.5 cm width.
She threads a lifeline every 20 rows and counts 47 stitches at the end of each right-side row.

Because the repeat adds and removes the same number of stitches, the scarf stays 47 stitches wide. When she drops a yarn over on row 53, she pulls back only to the lifeline at row 40, not to the start.
How to put in a lifeline

Thread a tapestry needle with smooth, thin cotton thread or dental floss in a contrasting colour. Pass it through every stitch on the needle, under any stitch markers, and leave long tails. If you must undo rows, pull the needle out and rip back: the stitches stop at the lifeline, ready to put back on the needle.

Reading a lace chart

Lace charts use an O or circle for a yarn over, a slash leaning right for k2tog and a slash leaning left for ssk; the slash shows the lean you will see on the fabric. Some charts include grey **no stitch** squares. These are not stitches at all; they hold the place of stitches that were decreased so the chart lines up. Skip them and go to the next real square.
Blocking lace

Unblocked lace looks crumpled, and many new knitters think they have made a mistake. Blocking opens it. Soak the piece in cool water for about 20 minutes, roll it in a towel to remove water, then pin it out on a clean flat surface: a bed with a sheet over it, foam play mats or a folded towel on the floor. Pin each point or edge to a measured shape, using rust-proof pins, and leave it to dry completely before removing pins.
**Cotton, linen and viscose blends** block well and hold the opened shape.
**Wool** blocks dramatically and keeps its shape well.
**Acrylic** does not hold a wet block in the same way. Light steam held above it can relax it, but too much heat flattens it permanently, so test on a swatch first.
Yarn overs at the edge
A yarn over before the first stitch or after the last stitch is easy to lose. That is why most lace patterns keep 2 or 3 plain stitches at each edge, as in Ruth's scarf.

Short rows: wrap and turn, German short rows and shaping for real bodies
Work wrap-and-turn and German short rows and hide the turns
Calculate how many short rows give a chosen extra length
Space turning points to shape a bust dart, a back neck or a curved hem
Choose between the two methods for a project

A **short row** is a row you do not finish. You knit part of the way, turn the work, and go back. The stitches you worked now have two more rows than the stitches you skipped. Done several times, with the turning point moving each time, this adds length in one area only. That is how knitters shape a bust, slope shoulders, raise a back neck and curve a hem without cutting fabric.
A woman's top
Short rows give a top extra length over the bust so the hem hangs level.
Method 1: wrap and turn (W&T)
On a knit row, work to the turning point. Bring the yarn to the front.
Slip the next stitch purlwise to the right needle.
Take the yarn to the back, then return the slipped stitch to the left needle. The yarn now wraps around its base.
Turn the work and purl back. On a purl row the moves are mirrored: yarn to back, slip, yarn to front, return, turn.
Later, when you reach a wrapped stitch on a full row, lift the wrap with the right needle and work it together with its stitch so the wrap is hidden on the wrong side.
Method 2: German short rows

German short rows are quicker and leave fewer gaps for many knitters. After you turn, bring the yarn to the front, slip the first stitch purlwise, then pull the yarn up and over the needle to the back. The stitch is pulled up and shows two legs; this is called a **double stitch**. When a full row reaches it, knit (or purl) both legs together as one stitch.

How many short rows?

Short rows are worked in pairs: one row out, one row back. Each pair adds **2 rows** in the worked area. So: extra length needed in cm x rows per cm = extra rows, and extra rows divided by 2 = pairs of short rows. Then spread the turning points evenly across the area that needs shaping.
Worked example: a short-row bust dart

For example, Ifeoma in Enugu is knitting a fitted top. The front is 100 stitches. After measuring, she finds the front needs about 5 cm more length than the back over the bust. Her gauge is 20 stitches and 28 rows per 10 cm. Her bust points are about 18 cm apart.
Extra rows: 5 cm x 2.8 rows per cm = 14 rows, which is 7 pairs of short rows.
Centre stitches between bust points: 18 cm x 2 stitches per cm = 36 stitches.
Stitches from each side edge to the bust point: (100 minus 36) divided by 2 = 32 stitches.
She spaces 7 turns inside those 32 stitches, about 4 stitches apart: turn 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 and 28 stitches from each edge.
Pair 1: knit to the last 4 sts, turn; purl to the last 4 sts, turn. Pair 2: work to the last 8 sts each side, and so on, to 28 sts.
She then works one full right-side row and one full wrong-side row, hiding all the turns.
The centre 44 stitches gain 14 rows (about 5 cm), and the side seams stay the same length as the back. The hem of her top now hangs level instead of rising at the front.
Turn only in the right zone
For a bust dart, the last turning point should stop a few centimetres before the bust point. If short rows run right across the bust point, the dart can form a pointed bump.

Intermediate crochet: motifs, tapestry, amigurumi and Tunisian

Crochet is fast, sturdy and well suited to bags, homeware, toys and light tops. This module covers four crochet families that sell well and build real skill: joined motifs, tapestry colourwork, stuffed amigurumi and Tunisian crochet. All crochet instructions in this module use US terms, with the UK name given where it helps.
Granny squares to size: counting rounds, planning a blanket and four joins
Work a classic granny square and predict its stitch count at any round

The granny square is a small motif worked in rounds from the centre out. Joined together, squares become blankets, bags, cushion covers and even cardigans. The intermediate skill is not making one square; it is making many squares that are all the same size, planning how many you need, and joining them so the seams look intentional.
A layout of square panels arranged in a grid
A blanket is a grid: plan rows and columns of squares before you start.
The classic square (US terms)
Round 1: magic ring. Ch 3 (counts as first dc), 2 dc in ring, ch 2. *3 dc in ring, ch 2* three times. Join with sl st to top of ch-3. You have 4 clusters of 3 dc.
Round 2: sl st to the first ch-2 corner space. In that corner: ch 3, 2 dc, ch 2, 3 dc. *Ch 1, then in the next corner: 3 dc, ch 2, 3 dc* three times. Ch 1, join. You have 8 clusters.
Round 3: corners as before, and 3 dc in each ch-1 space along the sides, with ch 1 between clusters. You have 12 clusters.
Every later round: one corner group in each corner and one cluster in each side space.

There is a pattern in the counts. Round 1 has 4 clusters, round 2 has 8, round 3 has 12. **Round n has 4 x n clusters**, which is 12 x n double crochet stitches. Round 6 has 24 clusters and 72 dc. If your count is different, you missed or added a cluster, and the square will twist or ripple.
Stop the slant

Squares worked always in the same direction can slowly twist. Some makers turn the square over at the end of each round and work the next round in the other direction. Whatever you choose, do the same for every square so they all match.

For example, Bisi in Akure takes orders for baby blankets. She makes one 4-round square in soft cotton-blend yarn, blocks it, and it measures 10 cm across. She weighs it on a kitchen scale at 9 g. The customer wants a blanket about 80 cm by 100 cm.
Squares across: 80 divided by 10 = 8. Squares down: 100 divided by 10 = 10.
Total squares: 8 x 10 = 80.
Yarn for squares: 80 x 9 g = 720 g.
She adds about 15% for joining and a border: 720 x 1.15 = 828 g.
Yarn comes in 50 g balls: 828 divided by 50 = 16.6, so she buys 17 balls, all from the same dye lot.
Bisi quotes the customer with a real yarn cost, and she knows she must make 80 identical squares. She makes 10 squares a day over 8 days, measuring a few from each batch against her first square.

In **tapestry crochet**, you work with two or more colours at once. The colour you are not using lies along the tops of the stitches and you crochet over it, so it is hidden inside the fabric. The result is a firm, dense fabric that holds its shape, which is why tapestry crochet is popular for bags, pouches, baskets and wall hangings. Geometric designs inspired by woven and printed cloth suit it very well.
A handbag
Tapestry crochet's firm fabric suits bags and pouches that must hold their shape.
The colour change
Work single crochet (UK double crochet) with colour A, laying colour B along the top of the row so each stitch wraps around it.
On the last stitch in colour A before the change, insert the hook and pull up a loop as usual, so you have 2 loops on the hook.
Drop A, yarn over with colour B and pull through both loops. The stitch top is now B.
Continue in B, now carrying A inside the stitches.
Keep both yarns at the back of the work so they do not twist into a tangle; turn the work regularly to untwist.
Keep the carried yarn hidden

If the carried colour peeps through, pull it slightly snug every few stitches, and use a hook a little smaller than you would for ordinary single crochet in that yarn. If the fabric becomes stiff like cardboard, go back up half a size.
Charts and stitch counts

A tapestry chart is drawn on squared paper: each square is one stitch, each row of squares is one row or round. Worked in the round, you read every round from right to left (left-handed makers usually read left to right). The chart repeat must divide exactly into the number of stitches in the round, or the pattern will break where the round starts.

Check the repeat: 60 divided by 12 = 5 diamonds around the pouch. It fits.
Sides: she stops increasing and works rounds of 60 sc, so the sides go straight up.
Height: she wants 15 cm of side. 15 x 1.2 rounds per cm = 18 rounds.

**Amigurumi** is the Japanese name for small crocheted stuffed toys and figures. They are worked mostly in single crochet in continuous spiral rounds, with no slip stitch join and no turning chain. A stitch marker in the first stitch of each round shows where the round starts. The fabric must be tight so stuffing does not show, so most makers use a hook smaller than the yarn label suggests.
A teddy bear
Every amigurumi body, head and limb is built from simple shapes: spheres, tubes and cones.
The six-increase sphere

Start with 6 stitches in a magic ring. On each increase round, add 6 stitches, spread evenly. Then work plain rounds, then decrease 6 stitches per round in the mirror image. This gives a ball. Change how many increase rounds you do and you change the size; change the number of plain rounds and you make an egg shape.

Round, not hexagon

If you put the increases in the same place every round, the sphere gets six corners. Stagger them: for example, on round 4 work (sc, inc, sc) 6 times instead of (2 sc, inc) 6 times. The stitch count is the same but the corners disappear.

Making toys safe
For babies and children under 3, **embroider eyes and noses with yarn** instead of using plastic safety eyes, buttons or beads. Small parts that come loose are a choking hazard.
For older children, safety eyes must have their locking washer pushed fully on from the inside **before** the piece is closed.
Use new, clean polyester toy stuffing, not old pillow filling, rags or foam pieces.
Sew limbs and ears on with the same yarn, going through the body several times, and weave the ends deep inside.
Give every toy a firm pull on each part before you sell or gift it. Avoid long cords or loops that could wrap around a neck.
Selling toys to shops or abroad

Toys sold in many countries must meet official safety standards (for example, EN 71 in Europe). If you plan to supply shops or export, ask the standards authority in the place you sell, such as the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) at home, what applies before you take bulk orders.

Stuff firmly but evenly, a little at a time, pushing stuffing into the edges with the back of a pencil. Under-stuffed toys sag; over-stuffed ones stretch the stitches and show white stuffing. Close the last 6 stitches by threading the tail through the front loops and pulling tight like a drawstring.

Limbs and ears are usually tubes. Start with 6 or 8 stitches in a magic ring, increase once or twice to the width you want, then work straight rounds until the limb is long enough. **Tunisian crochet** sits between knitting and crochet. You use a long hook, often called an afghan hook, and you keep many loops on it at once, like a knitting needle. Each row has two passes and you never turn the work. The fabric is dense and has a woven or knitted look, which suits scarves, dishcloths, bags and baby blankets.
A woman working on a creative project
Tunisian crochet is worked with the right side always facing you.
The two passes of Tunisian simple stitch (Tss)

Foundation: chain the number of stitches you need. Insert the hook in the 2nd chain from the hook, yarn over, pull up a loop and **keep it on the hook**. Repeat in each chain. You now have one loop per chain.
Return pass: yarn over and pull through 1 loop. Then *yarn over and pull through 2 loops* until one loop remains. This loop is the first stitch of the next row.
Forward pass (Tss): skip the first vertical bar. Insert the hook from right to left under the next front vertical bar, yarn over, pull up a loop. Repeat across.
At the end, insert under both strands of the last edge stitch for a firm edge, pull up a loop, then do the return pass as before.
Bind off: slip stitch under each vertical bar across the last row.

For **Tunisian knit stitch (Tks)**, insert the hook between the front and back vertical bars of each stitch, from front to back, instead of under the front bar. The result looks very like knitted stocking stitch, but is thicker. Tunisian purl stitch brings the yarn to the front before each loop, making a bumpy texture like purl.

Tunisian fabric tends to curl towards you, because the front is more crowded than the back. Most makers handle it in four ways together: use a hook noticeably larger than you would for ordinary crochet with the same yarn; start with a looser foundation chain (or a chain made with a bigger hook); add a border of ordinary crochet; and block the finished piece. Patterns with mixed stitches, such as Tss and Tunisian purl, curl less than plain Tss.
Wide pieces
A straight afghan hook holds a limited number of loops. For blankets, use a Tunisian hook with a flexible cable attached, or make the blanket in strips and join them.

Length: 150 cm x 1.5 rows per cm = 225 rows.
She times herself: 10 rows take 25 minutes, which is 2.5 minutes per row.
Total making time: 225 x 2.5 = 562.5 minutes, about 9.4 hours. She adds 1 hour for border, ends and blocking: about 10.5 hours.
She records the yarn used by weighing the finished scarf.
Mercy now knows each scarf takes about 10.5 hours. She will use that real figure, not a guess, when she prices for the boutique in Module 5.

The top-down raglan: calculating a seamless yoke

A **top-down raglan** starts at the neck and grows downward. Four diagonal lines, the raglan lines, run from the neck to each underarm. On increase rounds you add a stitch on each side of each line, so 8 stitches are added per round. When the yoke is deep enough, the sleeve stitches go onto waste yarn and the body continues alone. Because there are no seams, you can try it on at any point, which makes it ideal for fitting real bodies.
A simple top
Raglan tops have diagonal lines from neck to underarm and can be made with no sewn seams.
The plan in five stages
Cast on the neck stitches and join in the round. Place 4 markers to divide back, sleeve, front, sleeve.
Increase round: *knit to 1 stitch before the marker, make 1, k1, slip marker, k1, make 1* four times. That adds 8 stitches. Work a plain round between increase rounds.
If the sleeves are wide enough before the body, continue increasing on the body only (4 stitches per round).
Separate: put each sleeve's stitches on waste yarn and cast on a few stitches under each arm. Join and knit the body.
Return to each sleeve: pick up the underarm stitches, knit the sleeve in the round, decreasing towards the cuff.
Worked example: calculating a raglan yoke

For example, Chioma (from the last lesson) changes to a yarn with a gauge of 20 stitches and 28 rounds per 10 cm. Targets: neck 50 cm, finished bust 106 cm, sleeve top 36 cm, underarm cast-on 4 cm each side.
Neck: 50 x 2 = 100 stitches. She divides them: back 34, front 34, sleeves 16 each. Check: 34 + 34 + 16 + 16 = 100.
Body target: 106 x 2 = 212 stitches. Underarm cast-on: 4 cm x 2 = 8 stitches each side, 16 in total. So front and back from the yoke need (212 minus 16) divided by 2 = 98 each.
Front grows from 34 to 98: 64 extra stitches, 2 per increase round, so 32 increase rounds.
Sleeve target: 36 x 2 = 72 stitches, minus 8 underarm stitches = 64 from the yoke. 64 minus 16 = 48 extra, 2 per round, so 24 increase rounds.
Plan: 24 increase rounds on all four sections, then 8 more increase rounds on front and back only.
Yoke depth: 32 increase rounds, each followed by a plain round = 64 rounds. 64 divided by 2.8 rounds per cm = about 22.9 cm.

Her yoke will be about 23 cm deep, close to the client's 20 cm armhole depth plus ease. After separating, the body has 98 + 98 + 16 = 212 stitches (106 cm) and each sleeve 64 + 8 = 72 stitches (36 cm), exactly matching the schematic.

Finishing is where a handmade garment starts to look professional, and where many makers rush. Neat seams, an even neckband, buttonholes that line up and correct blocking can double how much a customer is willing to pay. Plan for finishing to take real time: for a cardigan it can be several hours.

Picking up stitches along an edge

For a neckband or button band, you pick up new stitches along an edge and knit outward. Stitches are wider than rows are tall, so you cannot pick up one stitch in every row. In stocking stitch, a common guide is **3 stitches for every 4 rows** (or 2 for every 3 rows), because typical gauges have roughly 20 stitches to 28 rows. Divide your stitch gauge by your row gauge for a more exact ratio.
Worked example: a button band with evenly spaced buttonholes

For example, Aisha in Ilorin is finishing a cardigan front edge of 130 rows. Her gauge is 22 stitches and 30 rows per 10 cm. She wants 6 buttonholes, each made by casting off 2 stitches, with 3 stitches left at each end.
Ratio: 22 divided by 30 = 0.73 stitches per row. 130 x 0.73 = 95 stitches. She needs a number that fits the buttonholes, so she checks nearby numbers.
Stitches not in buttonholes or ends: band minus 12 buttonhole stitches minus 6 end stitches. These must divide by 5, the number of gaps between 6 buttonholes.
For 98 stitches: 98 minus 12 minus 6 = 80, and 80 divided by 5 = 16. It fits evenly.
She picks up 98 stitches (very close to 95) and works the band in rib.
Buttonhole row: 3 sts, (cast off 2, work 16) 5 times, cast off 2, 3 sts. Check: 3 + 5 x 18 + 2 + 3 = 98. On the next row she casts on 2 stitches over each gap.
The six buttonholes are exactly 16 stitches apart, and the band lies flat because the pick-up number follows her gauge ratio. She sews the buttons on the other band opposite each hole.

Weaving in ends

Leave tails of at least 15 cm. Thread each tail on a tapestry needle and weave it on the wrong side through the backs of stitches, changing direction at least once so it cannot pull out. For slippery cotton and viscose, weave a little further. In crochet, you can also work over tails as you go. Trim close only after blocking, because fabric moves a little when wet.
Blocking by fibre
**Cotton, linen and viscose blends:** wet block; they can stretch when wet and heavy, so dry flat, never hanging.
**Wool:** wet or steam block. Never use hot water with rubbing or agitation, or it can felt and shrink.
**Acrylic:** do not press with a hot iron. Gentle steam held above the fabric can relax it, but too much heat flattens it permanently.
Pin the piece to the measurements on your schematic and let it dry completely, out of direct sun.

Steam can scald. Hold the iron above the fabric, never on it, keep hands clear of the steam, and keep the iron and cord out of reach of children. Switch it off at the wall when you finish.

Finally, add a care label: fibre content and washing instructions, for example 'Hand wash cool, dry flat, do not tumble dry'. The Craft Yarn Council publishes the standard care symbols found on yarn labels, so copy the instructions from your yarn's ball band. Customers keep garments longer when they know how to wash them.

Identifying unlabelled yarn

Market yarn is not always labelled. A small burn test tells you the fibre family. Snip about 5 cm, hold it with metal tweezers over a bowl of water or a sink, and bring it to a flame. **Plant fibres** (cotton, linen, viscose) burn steadily, smell like burning paper and leave soft grey ash. **Animal fibres** (wool) burn slowly, smell like burning hair and tend to put themselves out. **Synthetics** (acrylic, nylon, polyester) shrink from the flame, melt and leave a hard bead.
Burn test safely

Use only a short snip, hold it with metal tweezers never fingers, work over water away from fabrics and gas cylinders, ventilate the room, keep children away, and never test near a stove that is in use. Melting synthetics can drip and burn skin.

For example, Mercy (from Module 3) prices her Tunisian scarf. All naira figures are approximate examples, not market prices. Her scarf uses 180 g of yarn sold at about 2,500 naira per 100 g ball. A tag and packaging cost about 500 naira. It takes 10.5 hours. She sets her rate at 800 naira per hour, adds 10% overhead and 25% profit.
Yarn: 2,500 divided by 100 g = 25 naira per gram. 180 g x 25 = 4,500 naira.
Materials total: 4,500 + 500 = 5,000 naira.
Labour: 10.5 x 800 = 8,400 naira.
Subtotal: 5,000 + 8,400 = 13,400. Overhead 10%: 1,340. Full cost: 14,740 naira.

Materials and labour form the base; a price that skips any layer loses money somewhere.
Markup and margin are different

**Markup** is profit as a percentage of cost. **Margin** is profit as a percentage of the selling price. Mercy added 25% markup: profit is 18,425 minus 14,740 = 3,685 naira. As a margin, that is 3,685 divided by 18,425 = 20%. When a buyer asks for a discount, check it against margin: a 20% discount would wipe out all her profit.
Consignment and custom orders

In **consignment**, a shop displays your items and pays you only after they sell, keeping an agreed commission. To receive your wholesale price after commission, divide by what you keep. If a boutique keeps 30%, you keep 70%: 18,500 divided by 0.7 = 26,429, so the shop price should be at least about 26,500 naira. Agree in writing on the commission, who sets the shop price, how often you are paid, and what happens to unsold or damaged items.
For custom orders, take a deposit before you buy yarn, enough to cover materials at least, and agree the balance before delivery.
Write the order: size or finished measurements, colours, delivery date, price and deposit paid.
Raise prices for rush orders that push other work aside.
Batch similar items: making 10 pouches in a row is usually faster per pouch than making them one at a time, which improves your hourly earnings.
Re-time and re-price
Yarn prices change and you will get faster. Weigh and time a sample of each product every few months and update your costing sheet so your prices stay fair to you and your customers.

Check your price from the buyer's side as well. Look at what similar handmade items cost on Instagram, WhatsApp catalogues and at local fairs, and note the size, fibre and finish of each. If your calculated price is much higher, look for honest ways to reduce cost: a faster stitch, a smaller size, a cheaper but suitable fibre, or batching. If it is much lower, you may be undervaluing your time or your finishing. Do not simply copy the lowest price you see, because you do not know whether that maker is covering her costs.

Pattern anatomy
Scan six sections, in this order
Materials: yarn, needle or hook, notions
Gauge: stitches and rows in 10 cm
Instructions, with stitch counts

Read the pattern once, start to finish, before you cast on or chain.
Check the materials: can you get this yarn, and do you have the needle or hook? Then the gauge. Which stitch is it measured in?
Choose your size by finished measurement, not by the letter. Then circle every number for your size through the whole pattern, so you never read the wrong one mid-row.
Check the abbreviations, then the instructions. A stitch count at the end of a row, like 48 stitches, is your checkpoint. Count after every shaping row. Finally, read the finishing notes.
Common mistake
US and UK crochet terms differ
US pattern says
UK pattern says
Here is the mistake to avoid. The same name means different stitches. A US single crochet is a UK double crochet.
If you follow a US pattern with UK stitches, every stitch is one step too tall, and the piece grows longer and wider than planned.
Look for clues. US patterns use sc and hdc. UK patterns use htr, and say tension and miss instead of gauge and skip.
One square is one stitch
Row 1 is at the bottom, because fabric grows upward.
Find row 1 at the bottom
Flat: right-side rows right to left
Flat: wrong-side rows left to right
In the round: every row right to left
Keep a ruler above your working row
On a chart, each square is one stitch, and the key explains each symbol. Find row 1. It is at the bottom, because fabric grows upward.
For flat knitting, read right-side rows from right to left, and wrong-side rows from left to right.
In the round, read every row right to left, because you always face the right side. Keep a ruler above the row you are working.

Make a swatch you can trust
Swatch in the stitch the gauge line names, then wash it.
Same yarn, suggested needle or hook
About 15 cm square
Work the stitch the gauge names
Wash and dry it flat
Count across 15 cm, then divide
Gauge, called tension in UK patterns, is how many stitches and rows fit into 10 cm. Two women with the same yarn and needles can get different gauge.
Use the project yarn, and make the swatch about 15 cm square, because edges are always uneven.
Work the stitch the gauge line names. Then block it the way you will wash the finished item: soak, press out water in a towel, and dry it flat.
Measure across 15 cm and divide. Half a stitch per centimetre changes the size a lot.
Worked example
Funke's jumper: why 2 stitches matter
Pattern: 22 stitches per 10 cm, front 110
Her swatch: 30 stitches in 15 cm = 20
Pattern width: 110 / 2.2 = 50 cm
Her width: 110 / 2.0 = 55 cm
Fix: 3.5 mm needles, 33 in 15 cm = 22
For example, Funke in Ibadan is making a cotton jumper. The pattern gauge is 22 stitches to 10 cm on 4 mm needles, and the front is 110 stitches.
Her washed swatch has 30 stitches in 15 cm. That is 2.0 stitches per cm, or 20 per 10 cm.
The pattern front would be 110 divided by 2.2, which is 50 cm. Hers would be 55 cm. Front and back together, the jumper would be 10 cm too big around.
Her fabric is looser, so she goes down to 3.5 mm needles. The new swatch counts 33 stitches in 15 cm, exactly 22 per 10 cm. One evening of swatching saved the whole jumper.
Resizing
Three formulas for any size
Target width in cm x stitches per cm. Stitches per cm is your gauge divided by 10.
Target length in cm x rows per cm. Add length in plain sections, not in the shaping.
Yarn rises with stitches: 20% wider needs about 20% more yarn. Buy one dye lot.
When the sizes do not fit the body, you can resize. Start from the finished measurement you want, including ease, not the body measurement.
Stitches equal target width in centimetres times stitches per centimetre.
Rows equal target length times rows per centimetre. Add length in the plain section below the armhole.
And yarn rises with the stitches. Buy the extra from the same dye lot.

Round to a count that fits the repeat, then recheck the width.
Target back 56 cm x 2 = 112 stitches
Repeat: multiple of 6 plus 2
112 minus 2 = 110, not divisible by 6
Choose 18 x 6 + 2 = 110 stitches
Recheck: 110 / 2 = 55 cm
For example, Grace in Jos needs a cardigan back of about 56 cm. At 2 stitches per cm, that is 112 stitches. But her cable rib is a multiple of 6 plus 2.
112 minus 2 is 110, and 110 does not divide by 6. So 112 will break the pattern.
The nearest counts that fit are 110 or 116. She chooses 110 stitches, a back of 55 cm, which still gives about 8 cm of ease.
Never add one or two stitches in the middle of a repeat. Round to a count that fits, then recheck the width.

Swatch 15 cm, wash it, then measure

Why this matters

This module adds four knitting techniques that turn plain fabric into products people notice. Cables give texture. Colourwork gives pattern.
Lace makes light pieces for warm weather. And short rows shape a top to fit a real body.
Cables
Each crossing is four small moves
Front goes left, back goes right.
Slip stitches purlwise to cable needle
Hold it in front or at the back
Knit the next stitches firmly
Knit the stitches from the cable needle
Hang a marker on the crossing row
A cable is a few stitches knitted out of order. Slip the stated stitches purlwise onto a short cable needle, and hold it in front or at the back, as the abbreviation says.
Knit the next stitches firmly from the left needle, then knit the ones from the cable needle, pulling the yarn snug.
Hang a marker on the crossing row, so you can count rows to the next crossing.
Remember: a front cross leans left, a back cross leans right. Put C6B on the left rope and C6F on the right, and they mirror.
Cables pull fabric in, so always swatch the cable pattern itself.
Colourwork
Three methods, one rule each
Change colour at the start of a row. Carry yarn up the side for narrow stripes, cut it for wide ones.
One bobbin for each block of colour. Twist the old and new yarn at every change.
Two colours in a row. Keep floats loose, and catch any float longer than about 5 stitches.
There are three colourwork methods. Stripes change colour at the start of a row. Carry the yarn up the side for narrow stripes, and cut it for wide ones.
Intarsia is for large blocks and letters. Each area of colour has its own bobbin. At every change, pick up the new colour from under the old one, so they twist and no hole forms.

Stranded knitting uses two colours in a row, and the unused one floats behind. Tight floats pucker the fabric. Catch any float longer than about 5 stitches. Stranded fabric is double thickness, so in hot weather use it for bags and accessories.

Kemi plans a striped scarf

6 rows each of A, B, C = 18 per repeat

A plain scarf uses about 300 g, so each colour needs about 100 g. Yarn comes in 50 g balls, so she buys 2 of each, plus 1 extra. She buys 7 balls instead of guessing.
Lace
Check that every repeat balances
Each yarn over adds a stitch. Pair it with a decrease.
yo adds 1 stitch and makes a hole
k2tog removes 1, leans right
ssk removes 1, leans left
Net change 0: the scarf stays 47 wide
Lace is fabric with holes placed on purpose. A yarn over adds a stitch and makes a hole. k2tog removes one and leans right. ssk removes one and leans left.
For example, Ruth in Abuja counts one repeat of her scarf: yarn over, ssk, knit, k2tog, yarn over, knit. The net change is zero, so her 47 stitches stay 47 all the way up.
Each yarn over adds a stitch, so pair it with a decrease.

Read the chart with a ruler

Keep these habits. Count stitches on every right-side row. Thread a lifeline every 10 to 20 rows, so a mistake costs minutes, not days. When Ruth dropped a yarn over on row 53, she pulled back only to her lifeline at row 40.

Short rows
Ifeoma's bust dart
Each pair of short rows adds 2 rows. Stop before the bust point.
Needs 5 cm more length at the front
5 cm x 2.8 rows per cm = 14 rows
14 rows = 7 pairs of short rows
Turns about 4 stitches apart
One full row each way hides the turns
A short row is a row you do not finish. You turn early and go back, so one area gains length. For example, Ifeoma in Enugu needs about 5 cm more length over the bust.

Bisi plans a baby blanket

Single crochet: firm, for bags
Whip stitch: flat, for baby items

A slip stitch join gives a decorative ridge. A single crochet join is firmer, good for bags that take weight.

The round's stitch count must be a multiple of the motif width.
Carry colour B inside the stitches
Pull up the last A loop: 2 on hook
Finish the stitch with colour B
Zainab: base round of 60 stitches
60 / 12-stitch motif = 5 diamonds
In tapestry crochet, the colour you are not using lies along the tops of the stitches, and you crochet over it, so it is hidden.
To change colour, on the last stitch in colour A pull up a loop, so you have 2 loops on the hook. Then yarn over with colour B and pull through both.

For example, Zainab in Kano has a diamond motif 12 stitches wide. Her flat base adds 6 stitches each round, so round 10 has 60. 60 divided by 12 is 5 diamonds. It fits, so no motif breaks where the round starts.
Amigurumi
Stagger the increases, or the ball gets six corners.
6 sc in a magic ring
Add 6 stitches each round: 12, 18, 24, 30
Work plain rounds
Decrease 6 per round, in mirror order
Stuff firmly, then close the last 6
Amigurumi are small stuffed toys, worked in tight single crochet spirals with a marker at the start of each round.
Start with 6 stitches in a magic ring, and add 6 stitches every round: 12, 18, 24, 30.
Work plain rounds, then decrease 6 per round in the mirror order. Stuff firmly before the last round, and close it like a drawstring.
Stagger the increases each round, or the ball turns into a hexagon.
Toy safety
Make every toy safe
Embroider eyes and noses with yarn. No plastic eyes, buttons or beads that can come loose.
Use new, clean toy stuffing. Sew limbs on through the body several times.
Pull each part firmly before you sell or gift it. No long cords or loops.
Toy safety comes first. For babies and children under 3, embroider eyes and noses with yarn. Small parts that come loose are a choking hazard.
Use new, clean polyester toy stuffing, not old pillow filling or rags. Sew limbs and ears on through the body several times.
Give every toy a firm pull on each part before you sell or gift it, and avoid long cords that could wrap around a neck.
Tunisian crochet
Two passes, then time yourself
Time 10 rows and multiply. Use real time for pricing.
Forward pass: pick up loops, keep them
Return pass: work them off in twos
Larger hook and a border stop curl
Mercy: 10 rows take 25 minutes
225 rows: about 10.5 hours in total

Tunisian crochet uses a long hook and keeps many loops on it, like a knitting needle. On the forward pass you pick up loops. On the return pass you work them off, two at a time. You never turn the work.
Tunisian fabric curls. Fight it with a larger hook, a loose foundation chain, a border, and blocking.

For example, Mercy in Benin City makes scarves of 225 rows. She times 10 rows at 25 minutes, so 2.5 minutes a row. With the border and blocking, each scarf takes about 10.5 hours. She will price from that real figure, not a guess.
Key points
Remember
Weigh one square, then multiply
Fit the motif into the round count
Add 6 stitches each increase round
Embroider features for under-3s
Time 10 rows to know your real hours
To remember. Weigh and measure one blocked square, then multiply. Make the round count a multiple of the motif. Add 6 stitches each increase round.
Embroider features on toys for under-3s and pull-test every toy. And time yourself, so your prices use real hours.

From measurements to a finished garment: ease, yokes and bands.
This is the video for module four of Advanced Knitting and Crochet.
Why this matters
Where every skill comes together
Measure a real body
Choose ease on purpose
Calculate a seamless raglan yoke
Finish it like a professional
Garments are where gauge, resizing and shaping come together. You start with a real body, and you choose ease on purpose. Ease is the difference between the body and the finished garment.
Then you calculate a top-down yoke, and finish with neat seams, bands and blocking. Good finishing can double what a customer is willing to pay.
Measuring
Key measurements for a top
Bust at the fullest part, tape level
Waist, hip and back waist length
Cross back and armhole depth
Upper arm, wrist and arm length
Neck and garment length wanted
A top needs ten measurements. Take the bust at the fullest part, with the tape level all round. Then waist, hip and back waist length.
Add cross back, armhole depth, upper arm, wrist, arm length, neck, and the garment length she wants.
Measure over light clothing, explain each one before you take it, and keep the card private. Write the date, because bodies change.
How much ease at the bust?
About 2.5 to 5 cm of ease. For fitted cardigans and tops.
About 5 to 10 cm of ease. For everyday jumpers and cardigans.
About 10 to 15 cm for relaxed tops, 15 cm or more for oversized cover-ups.
A close-fitting top has about 2.5 to 5 cm of ease at the bust.
A standard fit has about 5 to 10 cm, for everyday jumpers.
Loose tops have about 10 to 15 cm, and oversized pieces 15 cm or more. Crochet stretches less than knitting, so many makers add a little more ease for crochet.
Worked example
Chioma turns a body into stitches
Finished measurement x stitches per cm = stitch count.
Bust 98 + 8 cm ease = 106 cm
Front and back: 106 / 2 = 53 cm each
53 x 2.2 = 116.6, rounded to 117
Upper arm 32 + 4 = 36 cm = 79 stitches
Draw it all on a schematic
For example, Chioma in Asaba is knitting a standard-fitting jumper for a client with a 98 cm bust. She adds 8 cm of ease, for a finished bust of 106 cm. Front and back are 53 cm each.
Her gauge is 22 stitches per 10 cm, so 53 times 2.2 is 116.6. She rounds to 117 to suit her rib. The upper arm is 32 plus 4 cm of ease, 36 cm, which is 79 stitches.
She draws front, back and sleeve as simple shapes, and writes every number on them. That schematic is her plan and her check.
Top-down raglan
Calculating a seamless yoke
Try the yoke on before you separate the sleeves.
Neck 100: back 34, front 34, sleeves 16
Each increase round adds 8 stitches
Front 34 to 98: 32 increase rounds
Sleeves need 24 rounds, then body only
Yoke about 23 cm deep
A top-down raglan starts at the neck. Four lines run to the underarms, and each increase round adds a stitch on both sides of each line, 8 stitches a round.
With a new yarn at 20 stitches per 10 cm, Chioma's 50 cm neck is 100 stitches: 34 back, 34 front, and 16 for each sleeve.
The front must grow from 34 to 98 stitches. That is 64 more, 2 per round, so 32 increase rounds. The sleeves need only 24, so after 24 rounds she increases on the body only.
With a plain round between increases, the yoke is about 23 cm deep. Before separating the sleeves, she slips the stitches onto a long cable and tries it on.
Bands and buttonholes
Aisha spaces six buttonholes
Pick up about 3 stitches for every 4 rows.
Edge of 130 rows x 0.73 = 95 stitches
Remove 12 buttonhole and 6 end stitches
Pick up 98, space holes 16 apart
Stitches are wider than rows are tall, so you cannot pick up one stitch per row. A common guide is 3 stitches for every 4 rows.
For example, Aisha in Ilorin has a 130-row edge. Her ratio is 22 divided by 30, about 0.73, so she needs about 95 stitches.
She wants 6 buttonholes of 2 stitches, with 3 stitches at each end. The stitches left over must divide by 5, the gaps between the holes. With 98 stitches, 80 are left, and 80 divided by 5 is 16.
She picks up 98 and spaces the holes 16 stitches apart. Then she checks the total adds back to 98.
Block by fibre
Blocking safely, fibre by fibre
Wet block. They stretch when wet and heavy, so dry flat, never hanging.
Wet or steam block. No hot water with rubbing, or it can felt and shrink.
Never press with a hot iron. Hold steam above, keep hands clear, switch off at the wall.
Weave in ends with tails of at least 15 cm, then block. Cotton and viscose stretch when wet, so dry them flat, never hanging.
Wool can be wet or steam blocked, but hot water with rubbing makes it felt and shrink.
Never press acrylic with a hot iron. Steam can scald, so hold the iron above the fabric, keep your hands clear, keep it away from children, and switch it off at the wall when you finish.
Pin each piece to your schematic and add a care label.
Key points
Remember
Finished size x gauge = stitches
Each raglan round adds 8 stitches
About 3 stitches for every 4 rows
Block by fibre; steam with care

To remember. Choose ease on purpose. Finished size times gauge gives your stitches. Each raglan increase round adds 8 stitches. Pick up about 3 stitches for every 4 rows. And block by fibre, using steam with care.

Design, price and sell your knit and crochet line.
This is the video for module five of Advanced Knitting and Crochet.
Why this matters
Skill alone does not pay
Fibres and products for a hot climate
A small, matching product line
Prices built from your own records
Good photos and safe payments
Skill alone does not pay. In most of Nigeria the weather is warm for much of the year, so bags, homeware, baby items, light tops and gifts usually sell more steadily than heavy jumpers.
This module shows you how to plan a small product line, price it from your own records, and sell it with good photos and safe payment habits.
Fibres
Match fibre to product and climate
Cotton: bags, dishcloths, baby items
Linen blends: light tops, table runners
Viscose blends: lace scarves, flowing tops
Acrylic: toys, bags, cushions
Wool: harmattan accessories
Cotton is breathable and absorbent, good for bags, dishcloths and baby items. Linen blends are cool and crisp. Viscose blends drape well for lace scarves and flowing tops.
Acrylic is affordable and colourfast, good for toys and cushions, but it is not breathable and melts under a hot iron. Wool is warm, best for harmattan accessories.
Safety first
A safe burn test for unlabelled yarn
Short snip, metal tweezers, over water. Children away.
Snip about 5 cm of yarn
Hold with metal tweezers over water
Paper smell, soft grey ash: plant fibre
Hair smell, puts itself out: wool
Melts to a hard bead: synthetic
Market yarn is not always labelled. A burn test tells you the fibre family. Snip about 5 cm, and hold it with metal tweezers, never fingers, over a bowl of water.
Work away from fabrics and gas cylinders, never near a stove in use, ventilate the room, and keep children away.
Cotton, linen and viscose smell like burning paper and leave soft grey ash. Wool smells like burning hair and puts itself out. Synthetics melt into a hard bead, and can drip and burn skin.
Product ladder
Good, better, best in one colour story
Good: coaster set, about 1 hour
Better: tapestry pouch, about 4 hours
Best: custom baby blanket, 15 hours or more
One colour story: cream, mustard, indigo
A product card for every item
Instead of making one of everything, choose a few products at three levels. For example, Tolu in Abeokuta plans a collection for weddings, naming ceremonies and gifts.
Her good item is a coaster set that takes about 1 hour and brings new customers in. Her better item, the main seller, is a tapestry pouch. Her best is a custom baby blanket with the baby's initial.

She uses one colour story, cream, mustard and indigo, so her photos look professional together. And she writes a product card for each, with yarn, hook, grams, time and size, so the 20th pouch matches the first.
Worked example
Pricing a Tunisian scarf
For example, Mercy prices her scarf: 180 g of yarn, 10.5 hours, at 800 naira an hour.
Yarn: 180 g x 25 per gram
Tag and packaging
Labour: 10.5 hours x 800
Overhead, 10%
Profit, 25% markup
Naira prices are approximate examples.
Handmade work is often underpriced because the maker counts only the yarn. A fair price covers materials, your time, a share of running costs, and profit.
Mercy's yarn costs about 2,500 naira per 100 g ball, so 25 naira per gram. Her 180 g cost 4,500, plus 500 for a tag and packaging.
Her time is 10.5 hours at 800 naira an hour: 8,400.
She adds 10 percent overhead, and 25 percent profit.
That is 18,425 naira, which she rounds to 18,500 as her wholesale price.
Know your numbers
Markup, margin and consignment
Profit as a percentage of cost. Mercy's 3,685 profit is 25% of her cost.
Profit as a percentage of price: 20%. A 20% discount would wipe out all her profit.
Shop keeps 30%? Divide by 0.7. 18,500 / 0.7 means a shop price of about 26,500.
Markup is profit as a percentage of cost. Mercy added 25 percent.
Margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price. Her margin is 20 percent, so a 20 percent discount would wipe out all her profit. Always check discounts against margin.

In consignment, a shop pays you only after an item sells, and keeps a commission. If it keeps 30 percent, divide your wholesale price by 0.7. The shop price should be at least about 26,500 naira. Agree the terms in writing.
Selling safely
From photo to a safe sale
Never dispatch until the money shows in your own app.
Daylight, plain background, no flash
Whole item, close-up, in use, with ruler
Listing: size, fibre, care, price, delivery
Confirm payment in your own app
Pack, label and send a thank-you
The buyer cannot touch the yarn, so your photo must do that work. Shoot near a window in daylight, on a plain background, with the flash off.
Take a set: the whole item, a close-up of the stitches, the item in use, and one with a ruler for size.
Your listing should answer size, fibre, care, price, delivery and lead time, so buyers stop asking the same five questions.
Fake transfer alerts and edited screenshots are common tricks. Confirm every payment in your own bank or wallet app before you dispatch, and never share an OTP, PIN or password.
Then pack neatly, add a tag and care card, and send a thank-you message.
Key points
Remember
Cotton and plant blends for warm weather
Burn test safely, over water
Materials + labour + overhead + profit
Dispatch only after payment shows

To remember. Choose cotton and plant blends for warm weather. Burn test safely, over water. Build a good, better, best ladder in one colour story. Price with materials, labour, overhead and profit. And dispatch only after the payment shows in your own app.
